extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining inventorship, priority (35 U.S.C. 102(g)), conception, reduction to practice, suppression/ concealment, joint inventorship, and related claim-preclusion/ownership doctrines during examination and interference practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request under 37 CFR 1.48(a) is required to correct any error in naming the inventors in the U.S. application as filed. Foreign applicants may misunderstand U.S. law regarding naming of the actual inventors, especially where priority is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind foreign applicants of the requirement for identity of inventorship between a U.S. application and a 35 U.S.C. 119 priority application (see MPEP § 201.13). If the inventive entity named in a U.S. application is incorrect and a 37 CFR 1.48(a) request is not granted/entered for technical reasons but the admission of error is uncontroverted, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) should be made. (MPEP cross-references: § 201.03.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executors of oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 are presumed inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The party or parties executing an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 are presumed to be the inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Driscoll v. Cebalo; In re DeBaun. Caveats: the inventor of an element per se and the inventor of that element as used in a combination may differ; between inventors, their word is normally taken as to who are the actual inventors when there is no disagreement. Use presumptions cautiously and consider context and dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must contribute to the conception of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold question for inventorship is who conceived the invention. Unless a person contributes to conception, he is not an inventor; reduction to practice per se is irrelevant to inventorship except in limited simultaneous conception/reduction scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: In re Hardee; Fiers v. Revel. For chemical compounds, general knowledge of anticipated properties is insufficient — conception requires a conception of the specific compounds claimed. Suggesting a desired result (without means) does not make one a co-inventor (Ex parte Smernoff). See MPEP §§ 2138.04–2138.05 for evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of ideas/materials is permitted if inventor maintains intellectual domination
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may consider and adopt ideas, suggestions, or materials from others (employees, consultants, third parties) so long as the inventor maintains intellectual domination over making the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: inventor may adopt ideas 'so long as he maintains intellectual domination of the work of making the invention down to the successful testing, selecting or rejecting as he goes.' (Morse v. Porter; New England Braiding Co. v. Chesterton). Note: adoption from others can become a derivation in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor is not required to personally reduce the invention to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that the inventor personally carry out reduction to practice; reduction to practice can be performed by others on behalf of the inventor, provided it does not require the exercise of inventive skill beyond the inventor's directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Fritsch v. Lin; In re DeBaun; Mattor v. Coolegem; Tucker v. Naito; Davis v. Carrier. Distinguish technicians who merely follow instructions (not inventors) from those who contribute to conception or inventive structure/steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Each named joint inventor must contribute to the conception of at least one claim; joint inventors may have worked at different times, made unequal contributions, or not contributed to every claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute: 35 U.S.C. 116. Joint inventorship requires some 'quantum of collaboration or connection' (e.g., collaboration, common direction, one building on another’s report, hearing a suggestion). Contribution to one claim suffices. For means-plus-function claim elements, a contributor of a disclosed means is a joint inventor as to that claim unless contribution was merely reduction to practice of a broader concept (Ethicon v. United States Surgical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship 'to another' and effect of differing inventive entities
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint application/patent and a sole application/patent by one of the joint inventors are different legal entities; issuance of an earlier-filed application as a patent becomes prior art for everything it discloses where inventive entities differ, except in limited situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: (A) if the later-filed claim is entitled to benefit of an earlier application under 35 U.S.C. 120 (overlap of inventors is permissible); (B) if subject matter developed by another and the claimed invention were owned by the same person, subject to assignment to same person, or involved in a qualifying joint research agreement meeting 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) & (3) at time invention made. In those situations, rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/103 or 102(g)/103, or 102(e)/103 (for certain filing dates) may be precluded by 35 U.S.C. 103(c) once evidence is of record. See MPEP §§ 706.02(l), 2146.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) provides that subsection (f) of 35 U.S.C. 102 will not preclude patentability where subject matter developed by another (that would otherwise qualify under 102(f)) and the claimed invention were owned by the same person, subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or involved in a qualifying joint research agreement, at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 103(c) to preclude certain 102(f)/103 or 102(g)/103 or 102(e)/103 rejections for applications filed on or after specified dates (see MPEP and statutory text). Ensure required evidence of ownership/assignment/joint research agreement is in the record before treating as preclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) grounds for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) may form the basis of an ex parte rejection if: (1) the subject matter at issue was actually reduced to practice by another before the applicant’s invention; and (2) there has been no abandonment, suppression, or concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception alone is not sufficient to qualify as prior art under 102(g); evidence of actual reduction to practice is required. Filing of an application is a constructive reduction to practice but does not itself provide the evidence necessary to show actual reduction to practice for an ex parte 102(g) rejection (see In re Zletz). Where evidence of actual reduction is generally not available in ex parte examination, many disclosures fall under 102(e) rather than 102(g). 102(g) subject matter may also be the basis for a 103 rejection in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements considered in determining priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining priority of invention under 35 U.S.C. 102(g), consider the respective dates of conception and reduction to practice, and the reasonable diligence of a party who was first to conceive and last to reduce to practice (including diligence from a time prior to the other party’s conception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence, conception dates, and reduction-to-practice dates are commonly applied in interference contexts but also arise elsewhere (see Amgen v. Chugai; New Idea v. Sperry). Time charts illustrate award of priority in different factual scenarios (e.g., constructive vs actual reduction, diligence intervals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference practice is based on 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) is the basis of interference practice for determining priority of invention between parties; interference is an inter partes proceeding to determine first to invent among parties naming different inventors or combinations of pending applications and unexpired patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference practice (35 U.S.C. 135; 37 CFR Part 41 Subparts D & E; MPEP Chapter 2300) determines which party is first to invent; subject matter claimed by the losing party is rejected under 102(g) unless the acts showing prior invention were not in this country. First-to-invent rules detailed (conception + reduction + diligence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 scope and its exclusion in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits an applicant to show an actual date of invention prior to the effective date of a patent or literature reference applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (e), except where interference practice applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings; if a domestic patent claims the same patentable invention, interference rather than a 1.131 affidavit is required (Ex parte Standish). Subject matter available only under 102(g) is inherently made before the applicant and is not open to further inquiry under 1.131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost interference counts are not per se statutory prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of an interference count alone does not make its subject matter statutory prior art to the losing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, lost-count subject matter that is available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used alone or in combination under 35 U.S.C. 103. See In re Deckler regarding res judicata and collateral estoppel where Deckler was denied claims that were patentably indistinguishable from a claim lost in interference even though the lost-count subject matter was not available for obviousness rejections under 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention 'made in this country' requirement for 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is limited to inventions that are 'made in this country' (per 35 U.S.C. 104).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of conception, reduction to practice and diligence must be demonstrated in this country (Kondo v. Martel). GATT/NAFTA amendments to 35 U.S.C. 104 permit establishing dates of invention in certain foreign WTO/NAFTA member countries on or after statutory dates (see MPEP § 2138.02). Lost interference counts can nonetheless affect rights by res judicata even if not statutory prior art under 102(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) makes available as prior art the prior invention of another who has not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it. An invention may be deemed abandoned, suppressed, or concealed if, within a reasonable time after completion, no steps are taken to make it publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conduct giving rise to abandonment/suppression/concealment: failure to file a patent application, failure to describe the invention in a publicly disseminated document, or failure to use the invention publicly. Correge v. Murphy and International Glass cited. Filing within one year of public disclosure is not an unreasonable delay (Correge facts). Determinations are fact-specific; courts have found varying timeframes reasonable/unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment from delay in filing (interference context)
rubrics_metrics.description: During an interference, an inference of suppression or concealment may arise from an unreasonably long delay between an actual reduction to practice and the filing of a patent application; such an inference may prevent a junior party from prevailing when relying on an earlier actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay alone is not always sufficient; whether delay is 'mere' is case-by-case (Peeler v. Miller; Paulik v. Rizkalla; Peeler). Rebuttals: show activity directed to perfecting the invention, preparing applications, commercialization efforts, or reasonable research completion time (Holmwood; Engelhardt; Bogoslowsky). Suppression/concealment need not be attributable to the inventor (Peeler). Distinguish suppression/concealment from abandonment (Steierman; Correge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception: definition, contemporaneous recognition, and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is 'the complete performance of the mental part of the inventive act'—the formation in the mind of the inventor of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as later applied in practice. Conception requires contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention and possession of every feature recited in the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Townsend v. Smith; Hiatt v. Ziegler; Gunter v. Stream; Coleman v. Dines; Hybritech v. Monoclonal Antibodies; Hitzeman v. Rutter. Conception must be corroborated by evidence and demonstrates knowledge of every limitation of the count. Hope or speculative expectation is insufficient (Hitzeman). Conception does not require the inventor to know the invention will work or to appreciate its patentability (Burroughs Wellcome; Dow Chem. v. Astro-Valcour).
